result: Phosphorylation of CENP-T at Thr11 and Thr85 by CDK1:Cyclin B enables recruitment of two NDC80 complexes. ITC experiments show that phosphorylated Thr11 and Thr85 peptides bind SPC24:SPC25 with affinities of 45 μM and 4 μM respectively, while phosphorylated Thr27 and Ser47 do not bind. SEC and EM data demonstrate that phosphorylated CENP-T can simultaneously bind two SPC24:SPC25 units and two full-length NDC80 complexes.
evaluation: Claims C39, C44-C47 provide converging biochemical evidence from ITC, SEC, and mutagenesis experiments demonstrating that phosphorylation at Thr11 and Thr85 is both necessary and sufficient for NDC80C recruitment. The stoichiometry is confirmed by SEC analysis of mutants (C49) and direct EM visualization (C5, C77). The in vitro findings are consistent with prior in vivo data (C48).

result: CENP-T directly binds MIS12C in a phosphorylation-dependent manner requiring Ser201. Mass spectrometry confirmed that Ser201 is phosphorylated by CDK1 in vitro and in mitotic cells. SEC experiments with synthetic peptides and full-length constructs demonstrate that phosphorylation at Ser201 is both necessary and sufficient for MIS12C binding, while Thr11, Thr85, and Thr195 are dispensable. AUC analysis confirms a 1:1 stoichiometry with measured mass of 159 kDa matching the theoretical 162 kDa.
evaluation: Claims C40-C42, C57-C62 provide strong convergent evidence from peptide binding, mutagenesis, SEC, and AUC experiments demonstrating that Ser201 phosphorylation is necessary and sufficient for CENP-T:MIS12C interaction in vitro. Mass spectrometry data (C54-C56) confirms this site is phosphorylated by CDK1. The stoichiometry is rigorously determined by AUC (C63-C64).

result: In vivo validation using ectopic lacO tethering shows that CENP-T phosphorylation at specific sites is required for recruitment of NDC80C and MIS12C to chromatin. The S201A mutant recruits NDC80C but not MIS12C, while the T11A-T85A double mutant fails to recruit either complex. Unexpectedly, the T195A mutant also prevents recruitment of both complexes despite being dispensable in vitro, suggesting Thr195 may contribute to phosphorylation efficiency or CENP-T stability in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C65-C68 provide cell-based validation of the in vitro findings, showing that the identified phosphorylation sites are functionally important for kinetochore assembly in vivo. The discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo results for Thr195 (C68) is acknowledged and a reasonable speculation is offered (C69). The data are consistent with prior studies (C65, C66).

result: Phosphorylated CENP-T recruits one MIS12C and three NDC80C complexes in a defined stoichiometry. SEC analysis of systematic CENP-T mutants demonstrates that wild-type CENP-T associates with MIS12C and NDC80C in a 1:1:3 ratio, single T11A or T85A mutants show 1:1:2 ratios, and the T11A-T85A double mutant shows 1:1:1 ratio. EM visualization directly confirms that CENP-T coordinates MIS12C and three NDC80Cs into a single complex. The CENP-T:MIS12C complex can also incorporate KNL1C.
evaluation: Claims C71-C73 provide systematic stoichiometry analysis using a complete set of CENP-T mutants analyzed by SEC, demonstrating the additive contribution of each phosphorylation site. The conclusion that MIS12C bound to phosphorylated CENP-T can also bind NDC80C (C74) is directly supported by reconstitution experiments. EM visualization (C77) provides direct structural confirmation of the 1:1:3 stoichiometry.

result: CENP-C and CENP-T bind competitively to MIS12C at overlapping sites, indicating they act in parallel pathways to recruit outer kinetochore components. The MIS12C3xA mutant that cannot bind CENP-C also cannot bind phosphorylated CENP-T. Fluorescence polarization shows both CENP-C and phosphorylated CENP-T peptides displace labeled CENP-C from MIS12C, with binding affinities of 128 nM and ~30 μM respectively. SEC experiments confirm that CENP-C can displace CENP-T from preformed CENP-T:MIS12C complexes. This competitive binding predicts that CENP-C and CENP-T recruit two distinct MIS12C molecules and up to four NDC80C complexes in a CDK-regulated manner.
evaluation: Claims C78-C84 provide multiple lines of evidence (mutagenesis, fluorescence polarization, SEC competition assays) demonstrating competitive binding of CENP-C and CENP-T to MIS12C. The binding affinities are quantitatively determined (C81-C82). The conclusion that binding sites are overlapping (C85) and that two distinct MIS12Cs are recruited (C86) logically follows from the competitive binding data. The model (C92) is well-supported by the collective findings.

result: Structural characterization of NDC80C and MIS12C:NDC80C complexes by electron microscopy. Metal-shadowed NDC80C shows a coiled-coil spanning 51 nm with an end-to-end length of 62 nm (corrected for shadowing), slightly longer than the 57 nm reported for yeast NDC80C. A characteristic kink in the coiled coil marks the NDC80:NUF2 region. MIS12C forms an 18 nm rod-like extension at the SPC24:SPC25 side of NDC80C.
evaluation: Claims C50-C53 provide quantitative EM measurements of NDC80C dimensions with appropriate correction for metal shadowing artifacts. The measurements are compared to prior yeast data (C52) and structural features are identified based on prior studies (C53). The MIS12C extension measurement (C76) is consistent with prior negative-stain EM studies. These are well-controlled structural measurements.

result: Extrapolation to kinetochore stoichiometry predicts that mitotic phosphorylation triggers recruitment of four MIS12Cs and up to eight NDC80Cs per CENP-A nucleosome. This is based on the finding that CENP-A nucleosomes recruit two CCAN modules due to pseudo-symmetry. Quantitative studies from prior work show that 215 CENP-C and 72 CENP-T molecules recruit 244 NDC80Cs and 151 MIS12Cs per kinetochore, with only 82 CENP-C molecules engaging MIS12C and CENP-T recruiting the remainder.
evaluation: Claim C93 is an extrapolation based on the in vitro reconstitution data combined with prior findings about CENP-A nucleosome stoichiometry (C38). While the logic is reasonable, this prediction has not been directly tested. Claims C94-C96 cite prior quantitative studies but do not represent new findings from this work. The extrapolation requires validation through direct measurement of kinetochore stoichiometry in vivo.

result: Prior studies have shown that CENP-T is flexible and stretches under tension. The N-terminal tail of CENP-T was observed as a 25 ± 13 nm flexible extension by atomic force microscopy, and the N- and C-termini were ~30 nm apart under tension but only ~4 nm apart without tension.
evaluation: Claims C97-C98 accurately cite prior findings from Suzuki et al. 2011 about CENP-T flexibility and tension-dependent stretching. These are established observations from the literature that provide context for interpreting the current structural findings. However, these are not new results from this study.

result: Background knowledge about kinetochore structure and function. These claims establish the biological context including the role of kinetochores in chromosome segregation, the structural organization of CCAN and KMN complexes, the requirement for CENP-C and CENP-T in NDC80C recruitment, and prior evidence that CENP-C and CENP-T recruit NDC80C through distinct mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C1-C37, C87-C90 accurately summarize established knowledge from the literature with appropriate citations. These provide essential background context for the study but do not represent new findings. The citations appear accurate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the field.

result: CENP-C recruits a single MIS12:NDC80 complex.
evaluation: Claim C3 is stated as a primary finding but is actually established knowledge from prior work by the same group (Petrovic et al., 2016) as indicated in the manuscript. This serves as a comparison point for the CENP-T findings but is not a new result from this study.
